note: Synthetic transcript written for evaluation; not a real person's words.
setting: Parents' adobe farmhouse with a patio and stone corral in a highland community above Urcos, Cusco, Peru, childhood until 1991

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: So, the house.

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: My parents' house, in the community, above Urcos, in Cusco. Quispicanchi province. High up, maybe 3,800 metres. I left in 1991 to study in the city. It was adobe, all of it, and the roof was ichu, the straw, the grass from the puna.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: How did you come in?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: There was a path up from the road, between the potato fields, and you came into the patio, the open yard, through a, well, there was no gate, just an opening in the pirqa, the stone wall. Sometimes my father blocked it at night. The opening was on the downhill side, facing, eh, east? The morning sun came through it. East, yes.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: And the house was around the patio?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: On two sides. Facing you, the long building, two rooms. And on the right, the kitchen, separate, its own little house. The left side was the wall of the corral. No, sorry, the corral was behind the long building. The left was only the pirqa and the eucalyptus tree.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: The two rooms?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: The left one was where we slept, all of us, my parents, me, my three sisters. The right one was the store room, for the potatoes, the chuño, the freeze-dried potatoes, the seeds, and the tools. And above the store room, under the roof, the marka, like a loft, where my mother kept the maize. We went up a ladder, a log with notches cut in.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: What was in the sleeping room?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: My parents' bed, a platform of adobe, a raised part along the wall, with the frazadas on top, the heavy wool blankets. We children slept on sheepskins on the floor, near the door. A wooden trunk, a baúl, my mother's. And one small window, high up, no glass, just a hole.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: The kitchen?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: Ah, the kitchen. Dark, smoky, no chimney. The q'oncha, the clay stove, low on the floor against the back wall, with two holes on top, no, three. And the cuyes, the guinea pigs, all over the floor. They lived in the kitchen, dozens of them, under the bench, in the corners. That's normal there, they like the warmth.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: Was there a door to the kitchen?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: A low wooden door, maybe one and a half metres, you bent your head. And next to the kitchen, outside, the fogón, no, the horno, the bread oven, mud, like a dome. We only used it for fiestas, for Todos Santos, the t'anta wawas, the bread babies.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: Where were the animals?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: In the corral, the kancha, behind the house, big, with its own stone wall, chest high. Sheep, maybe thirty, forty, and four llamas, and our cow. At night everything went in. In one corner a little thatched shelter for the lambs. I spent half my childhood counting those sheep.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: How big was the corral?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: Hmm. Bigger than the patio. Maybe twenty metres, twenty-five, long? I don't know. The patio was smaller, maybe ten steps across.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: Was there anything on the roof?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: On the roof of the long building, at the top, a small iron cross, and the two toritos, the clay bulls from Pucará, for protection. Everybody has them in Cusco. My father put them up when the roof was finished, there was a party for it, the wasichakuy, the roofing.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: Water?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: There was a spring, a pukyu, down below the fields, ten minutes walking. My sisters and I carried the water up every morning, and there was a big clay jar, a puyñu, by the kitchen door, that's where it went.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: And the fields?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: Around the house on two sides, potatoes and habas, broad beans, and above, on the slope, the barley. One more thing, the threshing floor, the era, next to the corral, a flat circle of packed earth. They threshed the barley there in July or so.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: Anything else you remember about the patio?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: A big flat stone by the sleeping room door, where my father sat in the evenings chewing coca. And the patio was where we spread the potatoes to make chuño, in June, with the frost. That's all, I think. It was a small place, really.
